title: The Harbourside Discovery Centre: Maps, Facilities and Guided Instructions
instructions: 本材料为模拟练习（非官方雅思考试，也不对应任何官方分数）。请先听四段录音（每段播放两遍），完成第1–40题。听力原文仅供核对，请先做题再读原文。所有填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，并遵守字数限制。
transcript:
SECTION 1: Social Dialogue

Receptionist: Good morning, Harbourside Discovery Centre. How can I help you?

Caller: Oh, hello. I’m planning to bring a school group next month, and I’d like some information about visiting.

Receptionist: Certainly. How many students are you bringing?

Caller: There are 28 students, aged about 14, and three teachers.

Receptionist: Right. Well, for school groups we usually recommend booking a workshop. They’re designed for groups of 10 to 30 students, so 28 is fine. Which subject are you interested in?

Caller: Something to do with maps, I think. The students are studying geography.

Receptionist: Then the map reading workshop would be perfect. It lasts about 90 minutes and takes place in the learning rooms on the first floor.

Caller: Good. And how much does it cost?

Receptionist: The workshop is £4 per student, and teachers go free. That includes admission to the galleries.

Caller: That sounds reasonable. What time does it start?

Receptionist: We can offer either 10 a.m. or 1 p.m. Which would suit you better?

Caller: The morning would be better, I think. We’re coming by coach, and we need to leave by 2.30.

Receptionist: Then 10 a.m. gives you plenty of time. You should arrive at 9.45 to check in. The meeting point is beside the ticket desk, just inside the main entrance.

Caller: OK. And is there somewhere for the students to leave their bags?

Receptionist: Yes, the cloakrooms are directly behind the ticket desk. Large bags must be left there. But please ask students not to bring valuable items, as we can’t take responsibility for them.

Caller: Understood. What about lunch? Can they eat in the café?

Receptionist: The café has only 40 seats, so it gets very busy at lunchtime. For school groups we usually suggest eating outside if the weather is fine, or using the picnic area in the courtyard. There are benches there.

Caller: That’s a good idea. Is the courtyard easy to find?

Receptionist: Yes, it’s through the doors at the back of the atrium, opposite the café. You can’t miss it.

Caller: Great. One more thing—do you send any preparation materials?

Receptionist: Yes, we’ll email a pack two weeks before your visit. It includes a map of the centre and some worksheets. A member of the education team will also contact you to discuss any special requirements.

Caller: That’s very helpful. So I just need to confirm the booking?

Receptionist: That’s right. I’ll send you a booking form by email. Please return it within seven days to secure the date.

Caller: Will do. Thanks very much.

Receptionist: You’re welcome. We look forward to seeing you.

SECTION 2: Social Monologue

Welcome to the Harbourside Discovery Centre. Before you start exploring, here is some practical information to help you find your way around.

The main entrance is on the ground floor, and as you come in, you’ll see the ticket desk straight ahead. To the left of the ticket desk is the information point, where you can pick up a free map. The cloakrooms are behind the ticket desk, and we ask you to leave large bags there.

The café is in the north-west corner of the ground floor, beside the temporary exhibition space. It serves hot and cold food until 4.30. The gift shop is on the opposite side of the atrium, next to the lifts. It stays open for fifteen minutes after the centre closes, so you can do your shopping at the end of your visit.

To reach the permanent galleries, take the main staircase from the atrium to the first floor. The Harbour Gallery is the largest gallery and runs along the western side of the building. In the centre of the gallery you’ll find a reconstructed fishing boat. To the right of the boat is the navigation section, and beyond that is a small room about local shipbuilding.

The learning rooms are on the eastern side of the first floor. They are used for school workshops, so they are not usually open to the public. Between the galleries and the learning rooms there is a corridor with photographs of the old market.

On the second floor, the south end has a viewing balcony with a view over the harbour. It is open only on weekends and during school holidays, and it closes at 4 p.m. Please note that the balcony can only be reached by a short flight of steps from the second-floor landing; the lift does not go there.

If you need assistance, wheelchair users can borrow a wheelchair from the ticket desk free of charge, but we recommend reserving one at least 24 hours in advance. There is an accessible toilet next to the cloakrooms on the ground floor, and another on the first floor at the end of the corridor near the learning rooms. A quiet room is available on the ground floor, opposite the café.

Guided tours run at 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. daily and last about 45 minutes. They are limited to 15 people, so please sign up at the ticket desk. Tours are included in the admission price. We ask you to gather at the meeting point five minutes before the start.

Finally, a reminder about opening hours. From April to September we open at 9 a.m. and close at 6 p.m. Monday to Saturday, and at 5 p.m. on Sundays. From October to March we open at 10 a.m. and close at 5 p.m., and we are closed on Mondays. On the first Tuesday of each month, we open late, at 11 a.m., for staff training.

Enjoy your visit!

SECTION 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: So, for today’s seminar, I’d like you to discuss the problem of land subsidence in coastal cities. Let’s start with the causes. Maria?

Maria: Well, the main cause in many cities is groundwater extraction. When water is pumped out, the ground compacts and sinks.

Tutor: Exactly. And what about natural causes?

Maria: Some places are sinking naturally, like parts of the Netherlands, because of peat soils. But that’s usually much slower.

Tutor: Good. Now, what solutions have been tried?

David: Sea walls and pumps. But in Semarang, the sea wall itself started to sink, so they had to raise it.

Tutor: That’s a good point. It shows that engineering solutions can have their own problems. What about stopping groundwater extraction?

David: That’s the most effective, but it requires piped water, which is expensive and takes time.

Tutor: Right. Now, how do scientists measure subsidence?

Maria: They use satellite technology, InSAR, which compares radar images over time. It can detect movements of a few millimetres per year.

Tutor: Yes. And why is that important?

Maria: Because it shows the problem is more widespread than we thought. Before satellites, surveyors could only cover small areas.

Tutor: Excellent. Let’s move on to the social and economic costs. David?

David: Buildings crack, roads become uneven, and drainage stops working. In Semarang, some neighbourhoods have been abandoned.

Tutor: And the cost?

David: One estimate says several billion dollars over the next few decades.

Tutor: OK. Finally, what about adaptation rather than prevention?

Maria: Some cities are building floating buildings or raised walkways. Jakarta is moving its capital partly because of subsidence.

Tutor: Yes. So, to conclude, what’s the most important message?

David: That prevention is cheaper than repair. Managing groundwater carefully is key.

Tutor: I agree. And it requires cooperation between government, industry and residents. Good discussion, everyone.

SECTION 4: Academic Lecture

Good afternoon. Today I’m going to talk about food waste and how it differs between richer and poorer countries.

First, some definitions. Food loss refers to food that is lost before it reaches the consumer—during harvesting, storage or transport. Food waste, on the other hand, refers to food that is thrown away by retailers or consumers. This distinction is important because the causes and solutions are different.

In low-income countries, most food loss happens after harvesting. Farmers may lack proper storage facilities, so grain is damaged by insects or damp. In high-income countries, by contrast, waste occurs mainly at the retail and household stages. Supermarkets may reject fruit and vegetables that don’t meet cosmetic standards, and households throw away food that has passed its date label.

Let’s look at some solutions. For storage, hermetic bags are a promising technology. They seal out air and prevent insect damage. Studies suggest they can reduce losses by up to 98 per cent compared with traditional methods. However, they are more expensive, and farmers need training to use them correctly.

Transport infrastructure is also crucial. In rural areas, poor roads mean produce can’t reach markets quickly, especially in the rainy season. Building all-weather roads and providing small-scale cooling at collection points can help. These investments are costly but can pay for themselves through increased sales.

In richer countries, changing consumer behaviour is key. Confusion over date labels is a common cause of waste. Research in the UK found that the average family throws away food worth about £700 per year. Better planning, such as making shopping lists, can reduce this. Technology, like mobile apps that remind households before food expires, is also helping. In Denmark, a popular app has helped reduce waste, though the exact impact is hard to measure.

Policy measures are important too. France banned large supermarkets from throwing away edible food in 2016. Other countries have set targets to halve food waste by 2030. However, enforcement is a challenge, and data is often incomplete.

To sum up, reducing food waste requires action at every level: farmers, transporters, retailers and consumers. No single solution is enough. A combination of technology, infrastructure, education and regulation is needed. The benefits—economic, environmental and social—are likely to be substantial.

Thank you. I’m happy to take questions.

grammar.title: 位置介词、顺序表达、比较与变化描述
grammar.explanation: 英语常用介词表示位置（如 beside, opposite, at the end of），用 first/then/finally 表示顺序，用比较级和变化动词（rise, sink, reduce）描述变化。
grammar.example: The gift shop is on the opposite side of the atrium, next to the lifts.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The café is ______ the north-west corner of the ground floor.
questions.explanation: 表示在某个角落内部用 in the corner。
questions.evidence: The café occupies the north-west corner

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sequence word: ______, visitors should gather at the meeting point; then the tour begins.
questions.explanation: 表示顺序第一步用 First。
questions.evidence: Visitors should gather at the meeting point

questions.prompt: Choose the correct comparative: The problem is ______ than previously thought.
questions.explanation: 比较级用 more + 形容词。
questions.evidence: more widespread than previously thought

questions.prompt: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence with a present perfect meaning (an ongoing process that has happened up to now): Parts of the city ______ by up to 25 centimetres in a single year.
questions.explanation: 现在完成时表示到目前为止发生的变化，强调结果对现在的影响。
questions.evidence: Parts of the city have sunk by up to 25 centimetres
